newsitem.title: CHINA: Moody's move seen flattening Korean yield curve.
newsitem.headline: Moody's move seen flattening Korean yield curve.

text.p: Korean bonds traded offshore were little affected by the latest bad news from a rating agency, but analysts said spreads could widen, particularly in the shorter end of the curve.
Moody's Investors Service said it might cut South Korea's Prime-1 foreign currency country ceilings for short term notes and deposits and its A-1 rating for long term bank deposits.
It affirmed Korea's A-1 foreign currency rating for bond obligations, while maintaining its negative outlook.

"Current spreads are quite reflective and realistic... investors have been anticipating bad news coming out of Korea," said Albert Jan Hofman, Head of Asian Fixed Income Research at ABN Amro Hoare Govett.

But Hofman said he would expect some flattening of the yield curve for Korean sovereign-related bank credits, as spreads widen more in the shorter end of the curve than in the longer end to reflect Moody's harsher action on short-term debt.

Moody's also said it had placed on review for possible downgrade four banks -- Korea Development Bank, Industrial Bank of Korea, Housing and Commercial Bank and Export-Import Bank of Korea -- that have the same ratings as the sovereign.
Korea has not issued sovereign bonds in international markets, but Korean banks and companies are active borrowers.
Traders in Asia said they see more room for spreads to widen on sovereign-rated Korean banks' one-year floating rate note issues, perhaps by "some five to six basis points."
There has been little liquidity in the top Korean bank's short-dated FRNs, one trader at a Japanese investment bank said.
For example, Industrial Bank of Korea paid 27 basis points for its one-year FRN completed last week and there has been almost no trade in the paper, he said.
A number of Korean banks have issued one-year paper this year to entice investors unwilling to take on longer maturities.
Hanil Bank recently launced an FRN that featured an option to put the notes back to the issuer after just three months.
Because Moody's affirmed Korea's long-term foreign currency bond ratings, bankers said longer-dated paper could suffer less.
Korea Development Bank's fixed-rate yankee bond due 2006 is currently consolidating at 92-95 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries.
The bond widened to 100 basis points on July 24 when Moody's revised to negative the outlook on Korean sovereign-rated banks, but the spread has since narrowed.
"We don't think it (Korean debt) is very attractive right now," said one Hong Kong-based banker, saying even the higher yields did not justify the risk.
"Maybe it'll get a bit more attractive. If it gets downgraded, we may start to have a look at it," he said.
Despite the bad news, analysts were still relatively sanguine on the outlook for Korea's sovereign-rated banks on the view that the government would not allow them to fail.
A few big banks dominated the Korean bank sector and a few big corporates dominated the corporate sector, so a bank failure would be "catastrophic," HSBC Markets said in a recent report.
"Accordingly, it will not be allowed to happen," it said.

One banking analyst pointed out that the sovereign-rated entities have performed much better than more troubled Korean banks, such as Korea First Bank, which has heavy exposure to defaulted conglomerates Hanbo and Kia.
For example, spreads between longer-dated Korea Development Bank and Korea First Bank bonds have widened out to 120 basis points from about 20 basis points since the start of this year, she said.
-- Hong Kong News Room 852-2843 6371
